rationale: B wins because it keeps turning the announcement into reportable questions instead of polishing Calm's preferred story. Its strongest move is "whether the 18% figure is a between-group difference or a within-group change," which is exactly the kind of proof gate that saves a founder from walking into a science reporter's blender. A is strong, but "a category threshold moment — not just one deal" reaches farther than the facts can carry without outside proof.
gaps_in_A: "a category threshold moment — not just one deal" overstates the evidence from one company announcement with three unnamed insurers.
"Coverage Was the Last Wall" is a punchy headline, but it smuggles in an access thesis without uptake, activation, or member-use data.
"funder effect persists even with arm's-length conduct" may be true in the world, but it is not established by the supplied update; A should frame it as a question, not a premise.
The first two angles are a little too close: "Wellness-to-Clinical Shift" and "Coverage Was the Last Wall" both ride the same payer-coverage horse.
gaps_in_B: "at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply" is not in the supplied facts; B later admits this backdrop was not supplied, so it should not appear in the angle body.
"on the plan's dime" implies payment mechanics the update explicitly does not disclose.
"whether B2C consumer wellness has stopped growing on its own" is a useful business question, but it needs subscriber trend data before it becomes more than a reporter prompt.
